questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about the holy scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Although the light of nature, and the works of creation and providence, do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom, and power of God, as to leave men inexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God, and of his will, which is necessary unto salvation; therefore it pleased the Lord, at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that his will unto his Church; and afterwards, for the better preserving and propagating of the truth, and for the more sure establishment and comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan and of the world, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the holy Scripture to be most necessary; those former ways of God's revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the name of holy Scripture, or the Word of God written, are now contained all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi; Of the New Testament: The Gospels according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, John. The Acts of the Apostles, Paul's Epistles to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, The Epistle to the Hebrews, The Epistle of James, The First and Second Epistles of Peter, The First, Second, and Third Epistles of John, The Epistle of Jude, The Revelation. All which are given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life. The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture; and therefore are of no authority in the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings. The authority of the holy Scripture, for which it ought to be believed and obeyed, dependeth not upon the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself), the Author thereof; and therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church to an high and reverent esteem of the holy Scripture; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the doctrine, the majesty of the style, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God), the full discovery it makes of the only way of man's salvation, the many other incomparable excellencies, and the entire perfection thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence itself to be the Word of God; yet, notwithstanding, our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts. The whole counsel of God, concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men. Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word; and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed, for salvation, are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew (which was the native language of the people of God of old), and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the nations), being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them. But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God who have right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded, in the fear of God, to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every nation unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and, through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any scripture (which is not manifold, but one), it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly. The Supreme Judge, by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), written in 1646, is the most influential doctrinal standard in the Reformed Protestant tradition. Its first chapter, titled "Of Holy Scripture," is widely considered one of the most important and beautifully articulated statements on the doctrine of Scripture in the history of the Christian church. 

Here is a breakdown of what the Westminster Confession teaches about Holy Scripture, organized by its major themes:

### 1. The Necessity of Scripture (Section 1)
The Confession begins by acknowledging "General Revelation"—that God reveals His existence, power, and glory through nature and providence. However, it states that general revelation is insufficient to give people the specific knowledge they need for salvation. Therefore, God chose to reveal Himself through words and deeds, and to commit this revelation to writing. This makes the Bible **necessary** so that the truth might be preserved, propagated, and established against the corruption of human flesh and the malice of Satan.

### 2. The Canon of Scripture (Sections 2-3)
The Confession explicitly lists the 66 books of the Protestant Bible (39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament) as the complete canon of Holy Scripture. 
* **Exclusion of the Apocrypha:** It explicitly denies the divine authority of the Apocrypha (the deuterocanonical books accepted by the Roman Catholic Church), stating they are merely human writings and not part of the canon of Scripture.

### 3. The Inspiration and Authority of Scripture (Sections 4-5)
* **Divine Inspiration:** The Confession teaches that the Scriptures were given by the inspiration of God. God guided the human authors so that what they wrote was exactly what God intended. 
* **Self-Attesting Authority:** The authority of the Bible does not depend on the testimony of any man or church, but entirely upon God, its Author. Because God is truth itself, the Bible is immediately authoritative. 
* **The Work of the Holy Spirit:** While the church may bear witness to the Bible's authority, a person's full persuasion and assurance of its infallible truth and divine origin comes only from the "inward work of the Holy Spirit bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts."

### 4. The Sufficiency of Scripture (Section 6)
The Confession strongly asserts the **Sufficiency of Scripture**: "The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man's salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture."
* **No New Revelation:** Nothing is to be added to the Bible, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men.
* **Circumstantial Matters:** It acknowledges that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God and the government of the church that are not explicitly laid out in Scripture (e.g., what time to meet, building architecture). These are to be ordered by the "light of nature and Christian prudence," but always according to the general rules of the Word.

### 5. The Clarity (Perspicuity) of Scripture (Section 7)
The Confession teaches that not all parts of the Bible are equally easy to understand, and some require diligent study. However, it affirms that the things necessary for salvation are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or another, that both the learned and the unlearned can understand them through the ordinary use of means (like reading and hearing the Word).

### 6. Translation and Accessibility (Section 8)
Contrasting with the Roman Catholic practice of the time (which restricted the Bible to the Latin Vulgate), the Confession argues that the Bible must be translated into the common languages of the people. Because people need to search the Scriptures and worship God in a language they understand, the Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek are to be translated into the "vulgar" (common) language of every nation to which they come.

### 7. The Infallible Rule of Interpretation (Section 9)
The Confession establishes a foundational principle of Reformed hermeneutics: **Scripture interprets Scripture** (*analogia fidei* or analogy of faith). 
* The infallible rule for interpreting the Bible is the Bible itself.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), written in 1646, is one of the most influential doctrinal standards in Reformed theology. Its teachings about God and the Trinity are found primarily in **Chapter 2: "Of God, and of the Holy Trinity."** 

The Confession’s teachings are deeply rooted in classical Christian orthodoxy, but they emphasize specific Reformed distinctives, particularly God’s absolute sovereignty, self-sufficiency, and transcendence.

Here is a breakdown of what the WCF teaches about God and the Holy Trinity:

---

### Part 1: The Being and Attributes of God (Chapter 2, Sections 1–2)

The Confession begins by establishing the existence of God and then systematically defines His nature through His attributes. It divides these attributes into two categories: God's "incommunicable" attributes (those unique to Him) and His "communicable" attributes (those He shares with humanity in a finite way, like goodness and wisdom).

**1. The Unity and Simplicity of God**
*   **Only One True God:** The WCF affirms strict monotheism, stating there is only "one living and true God."
*   **Without Body, Parts, or Passions:** This is a crucial philosophical and theological statement. It means God is *simple* (not made up of different parts that can be divided) and *immaterial* (He is Spirit, not a physical being). "Without passions" does not mean God is apathetic; rather, it means He is not subject to fluctuating, reactive emotions or suffering against His will, as humans are. He is utterly constant.

**2. The Incommunicable Attributes (God's Transcendence)**
These attributes highlight the infinite gap between the Creator and the creation:
*   **Self-Existence (Aseity):** God has "life in himself." He depends on nothing outside of Himself for His existence, power, or happiness.
*   **Immutability:** God is unchangeable. He does not grow, evolve, or shift in His nature or decrees.
*   **Eternity & Immensity:** God is eternal (outside of time) and immense (outside of space; His presence fills the universe without being contained by it).
*   **Incomprehensible & Infinite:** God is beyond full human comprehension, and His perfections have no limits.
*   **Sovereign Freedom:** He is "most free," meaning He does whatever He pleases, constrained only by His own perfect nature.

**3. The Communicable Attributes (God's Moral Perfection)**
These attributes describe how God relates to His creation:
*   **Holiness:** He is "most holy," completely set apart from sin.
*   **Knowledge & Wisdom:** He is "most wise" and possesses infinite knowledge. The Confession explicitly states that God knows all things, including the future contingent actions of His creatures, because He has decreed them.
*   **Goodness & Love:** He is "most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity."
*   **Justice & Wrath:** He is "most just and terrible in his judgments, hating all sin, and who will by no means clear the guilty." The WCF holds God's mercy and His strict justice in perfect balance.

---

### Part 2: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity (Chapter 2, Section 3)

After establishing the nature of the one God, the Confession immediately addresses the Trinity to guard against the error of making God too distant or abstract. 

**1. The Unity of Essence**
The WCF states that in the Godhead, there are "three Persons, of one substance, power, and eternity." This means:
*   There is only one divine essence (substance). There are not three gods (Tritheism).
*   All three Persons possess the exact same divine power and have existed eternally. There is no hierarchy of being or time within the Trinity (unlike the heresy of Subordinationism).

**2. The Plurality of Persons**
The one divine essence subsists in three distinct Persons: **God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost.**
*   These are not just three modes or masks that one God wears (which is the heresy of Modalism). They are distinct, relational Persons.
*

questions.reference_answer: God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass; yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established. Although God knows whatsoever may or can come to pass upon all supposed conditions, yet hath he not decreed anything because he foresaw it as future, or as that which would come to pass upon such conditions. By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others fore-ordained to everlasting death. These angels and men, thus predestinated and fore-ordained, are particularly and unchangeably designed; and their number is so certain and definite that it can not be either increased or diminished. Those of mankind that are predestinated unto life, God, before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ, unto everlasting glory, out of his mere free grace and love, without any foresight of faith or good works, or perseverance in either of them, or any other thing in the creature, as conditions, or causes moving him thereunto; and all to the praise of his glorious grace. As God hath appointed the elect unto glory, so hath he, by the eternal and most free purpose of his will, fore-ordained all the means thereunto. Wherefore they who are elected, being fallen in Adam, are redeemed by Christ, are effectually called unto faith in Christ by his Spirit working in due season; are justified, adopted, sanctified, and kept by his power through faith unto salvation. Neither are any other redeemed by Christ, effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the elect only. The rest of mankind God was pleased, according to the unsearchable counsel of his own will, whereby he extendeth or withholdeth mercy as he pleaseth, for the glory of his sovereign power over his creatures, to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin, to the praise of his glorious justice. The doctrine of this high mystery of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care, that men attending the will of God revealed in his Word, and yielding obedience thereunto, may, from the certainty of their effectual vocation, be assured of their eternal election. So shall this doctrine afford matter of praise, reverence, and admiration of God; and of humility, diligence, and abundant consolation to all that sincerely obey the gospel.

The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), written in 1646, is the foundational doctrinal standard for Reformed theology. Its teaching on God’s eternal decree is found primarily in **Chapter 3**, which is arguably one of the most important and distinctively Reformed chapters in the entire document. 

The Confession teaches that before God created the world, He determined everything that would come to pass, doing so freely, perfectly, and for His own glory. This includes both the election of some to salvation and the passing over of others in judgment.

Here is a breakdown of the specific teachings regarding God’s eternal decree in the Westminster Confession:

### 1. The Nature of the Decree (Sovereign, Eternal, and Unchangeable)
The Confession opens by stating that God, from all eternity, did "freely, and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass." 
* **Eternal:** The decree was made before the foundation of the world.
* **Freely:** God was not constrained by anything outside of Himself. He did not have to create, nor was He obligated to save anyone.
* **Unchangeable:** Because God is perfectly wise and cannot err, and perfectly powerful and cannot be hindered, His decree cannot fail or be altered.

### 2. God’s Foreknowledge vs. Human Choice
A crucial aspect of the WCF is its rejection of the idea that God's decree is based on His foreknowledge of human choices. The Confession states that God's knowledge of future events is entirely dependent on His decree. He does not foresee things that might happen independently of Him; rather, He knows what *will* happen because He has decreed it to happen. 

Furthermore, the Confession insists that God's absolute decree does not violate the will of creatures or remove the reality of second causes (cause and effect). God ordains the ends *and* the means, but humans still make genuine choices for which they are morally responsible.

### 3. God is Not the Author of Sin
Because the Confession teaches that God has foreordained "whatsoever comes to pass," it anticipates the obvious objection: Does this make God the author of evil? The WCF emphatically says **no**. It states that God is not the author of sin, nor does He offer violence to the will of creatures. The Confession does not explain *how* God can sovereignly decree all things without being the author of sin, but it maintains that both truths are taught in Scripture and must be held together.

### 4. Unconditional Election
The Confession teaches that before the world was made, God chose a specific number of people to be saved. This election is:
* **Unconditional:** It is not based on foreseen faith, foreseen works, or any virtue in the person. It is based solely on "His mere free grace and love."
* **Christ-Centered:** God chose the elect to be redeemed by Christ, and He also ordained the means of their salvation—namely, that they would be effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and glorified.

### 5. Reprobation (Passing Over the Non-Elect)
The WCF also teaches the doctrine of reprobation—God's decree regarding those who are not elect. The Confession is very careful in its language here, distinguishing between how God relates to the elect and the non-elect:
* **Passive regarding sin:** God did not create the non-elect for the purpose of damning them, nor does He force them to sin. Rather, He "passes by" them and withholds the grace of salvation, leaving them in their own sin.
* **Active regarding judgment:** God actively decrees to punish the non-elect for their actual sins, to the praise of His glorious justice.

### 6. The Certainty of Salvation

The almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God so far manifest themselves in his providence that it extendeth itself even to the first fall, and all other sins of angels and men, and that not by a bare permission, but such as hath joined with it a most wise and powerful bounding, and otherwise ordering and governing of them, in a manifold dispensation, to his own holy ends; yet so as the sinfulness thereof proceedeth only from the creature, and not from God; who, being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be the author or approver of sin. The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave for a season his own children to manifold temptations and the corruption of their own hearts, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they be humbled; and to raise them to a more close and constant dependence for their support unto himself, and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for sundry other just and holy ends. As for those wicked and ungodly men whom God, as a righteous judge, for former sins, doth blind and harden, from them he not only withholdeth his grace, whereby they might have been enlightened in their understandings and wrought upon in their hearts, but sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had, and exposeth them to such objects as their corruption makes occasion of sin; and withal, gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan; whereby it comes to pass that they harden themselves, even under those means which God useth for the softening of others. As the providence of God doth, in general, reach to all creatures, so, after a most special manner, it taketh care of his Church, and disposeth all things to the good thereof.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), one of the most influential documents in Reformed theology, outlines its doctrine of providence in **Chapter 5: Of Providence**. 

The WCF teaches a robust, exhaustive view of God’s providence, asserting that God did not create the universe and then leave it to run on its own (Deism), but actively sustains and governs every detail of it. However, it does so with great care to preserve human responsibility and God’s holiness.

Here is a breakdown of the Westminster Confession’s teaching on providence:

### 1. The Scope and Basis of Providence (Paragraph 1)
The Confession teaches that God, the great Creator, upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures, actions, and things—from the greatest to the smallest. This governance flows from **God’s infallible foreknowledge** and the **free and immutable counsel of His own will**. 
*   **The Purpose:** All things are directed to the praise of the glory of His wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy.
*   **The Certainty:** Because providence is based on God's unchangeable will, nothing is left to chance. 

### 2. Primary and Secondary Causes (Paragraph 2 & 3)
A crucial concept in the WCF is the relationship between the "First Cause" (God) and "secondary causes" (created beings and natural laws). 
*   **Orderly Connection:** God is the First Cause of all things, but He uses secondary causes to accomplish His will. The Confession states that according to the nature of second causes, God makes them act necessarily, freely, or contingently. 
*   **Human Freedom:** This means that human choices are *free* choices (contingent causes), yet they are perfectly governed by God’s primary causation. God’s sovereignty does not violate the will of the creature.
*   **Working With, Without, and Against Means:** God normally works through ordinary means (the laws of nature, human effort). However, He is not bound by them. He can work *without* means (miracles), *above* means, or even *against* means (overruling the normal laws of nature to accomplish His purpose).

### 3. Providence and Sin (Paragraph 4)
One of the most difficult theological problems is how a holy God governs a world full of sin. The WCF addresses this with extreme precision:
*   **Permission, Not Authorship:** God is not the author of sin, nor does He have any fellowship with it. Sin proceeds entirely from the creature, not from God.
*   **Sovereign Limitation:** God permits sin to happen, but He bounds and limits it. 
*   **Ordaining Sin for Good:** The Confession states that God, in His sovereign wisdom, orders and governs sin to achieve His own most holy ends. (The classic biblical example is the crucifixion: the sinful actions of Judas and Pilate were ordained by God to accomplish the redemption of the world, yet the sin belongs solely to the men who committed it).

### 4. Providence Toward the Wicked (Paragraph 5)
The WCF teaches that God exercises a specific providence over the wicked:
*   **Withholding Grace:** God sometimes withholds His grace from the wicked, leaving them to their own depravity.
*   **Hardening:** He sometimes hardens their hearts (as He did with Pharaoh).
*   **Withdrawing Gifts:** He may withdraw the gifts they once possessed.
*   **Giving Them Over:** He exposes them to temptations and gives them over to their own lusts and the deceitfulness of sin. 
*   **Purpose:** This is done as a just judgment for their sins, to punish them for past sins, or to reveal the depth

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about god's covenant with man?
questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the creature is so great that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward but by some voluntary condescension on God's part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant. The first covenant made with man was a covenant of works, wherein life was promised to Adam, and in him to his posterity, upon condition of perfect and personal obedience. Man by his fall having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace: wherein he freely offered unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them faith in him that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto life his Holy Spirit, to make them willing and able to believe. This covenant of grace is frequently set forth in the Scripture by the name of a testament, in reference to the death of Jesus Christ the testator, and to the everlasting inheritance, with all things belonging to it, therein bequeathed. This covenant was differently administered in the time of the law and in the time of the gospel: under the law it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews, all fore-signifying Christ to come, which were for that time sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they had full remission of sins and eternal salvation; and is called the Old Testament. Under the gospel, when Christ the substance was exhibited, the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; which, though fewer in number, and administered with more simplicity and less outward glory, yet in them it is held forth in more fulness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy, to all nations, both Jews and Gentiles; and is called the New Testament. There are not, therefore, two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same under various dispensations.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), formulated in 1646, is the foundational doctrinal standard for Presbyterian and Reformed churches. Its teaching on God’s covenant with man is found primarily in **Chapter 7**, which is one of the most important articulations of Reformed "Covenant Theology." 

The Confession teaches that God relates to humanity entirely through the framework of covenants. Here is a breakdown of what the WCF teaches about God's covenants:

### 1. The Necessity of the Covenant (WCF 7.1)
The Confession begins by explaining *why* God makes a covenant with man. Because God is the infinite Creator and man is a finite creature, there is an immense distance between them. Man, as a creature, has no right to claim anything from God—not even life or blessing. Therefore, God must voluntarily "condescend" to man. God’s condescension is His gracious willingness to initiate a relationship with man by making a covenant, giving man a framework by which he can receive blessings from God.

### 2. The Covenant of Works (WCF 7.2)
The WCF teaches that the first covenant God made with man was the **Covenant of Works** (sometimes called the Covenant of Life). 
* **Parties:** God and Adam, who acted as the representative (federal head) of all humanity.
* **Condition:** Perfect and personal obedience to God's law (specifically, the command not to eat of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil).
* **Promise:** Eternal life and continued blessedness upon obedience.
* **Penalty:** Death upon disobedience.
Although the term "Covenant of Works" is not explicitly used in Genesis, the Confession sees it as necessarily implied by the structure of the law, the threat of death, and the promise of life.

### 3. The Covenant of Grace (WCF 7.3)
Because Adam broke the Covenant of Works, bringing sin and death upon all humanity, God could have justly left mankind to perish. Instead, God freely chose to make a second covenant: the **Covenant of Grace**.
* **Purpose:** To bring sinners to salvation and eternal life.
* **Mediator:** Jesus Christ. Because fallen man cannot fulfill the conditions of the covenant, Christ acts as the mediator and the federal head of the elect.
* **Condition:** Faith in Jesus Christ. The requirement for man is no longer perfect obedience to earn salvation, but trusting in Christ's obedience and sacrifice.
* **The Role of the Holy Spirit:** The Confession notes that God requires faith, but He also promises to give the Holy Spirit to the elect, working that faith in their hearts so they are able to believe.

### 4. The Two Administrations of the Covenant of Grace (WCF 7.4-5)
A crucial aspect of the WCF’s teaching is that there is only **one** Covenant of Grace across all of history, but it is administered in two different ways:
* **The Old Testament Administration:** Under the Law, the Covenant of Grace was administered through promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the Passover lamb, and other types and ordinances. These were "shadows" pointing forward to Christ. The Confession states that these Old Testament ordinances were sufficient to point the elect to Christ and offer them salvation, even though they lived before Christ was born.
* **The New Testament Administration:** Under the Gospel, the covenant is administered much more simply and clearly. The shadows have been replaced by the reality: the preaching of the Word, and the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. The Confession notes that the New Testament era has a greater "fullness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy" than the Old Testament era.

### 5. The Particularity of the Covenant (WCF 7.6)
Finally, the Confession addresses the scope of the Covenant of Grace. While the gospel is to be preached freely to all people, the Covenant of Grace itself is not made with every single individual without exception. It is made specifically with Jesus Christ, and in Him, with the **elect**—those whom God has chosen for salvation. God gives the Holy Spirit only to the elect to ensure they will ultimately be saved.

### Summary
In short, the Westminster Confession teaches that God's relationship with man is entirely covenantal. Adam failed the **Covenant of Works**, dooming humanity. In love, God initiated the **Covenant of Grace**, in which Jesus Christ fulfills the demands of the law and takes the penalty for sin, granting eternal life to all who have faith in Him—a faith that God Himself provides through the Holy Spirit.

Here is a breakdown of what the Westminster Confession teaches about Christ as the Mediator:

### 1. The Necessity and Appointment of the Mediator (Section 1)
The Confession teaches that because of the fall, humans are completely unable to justify themselves before God. Out of His eternal love and grace, God the Father **appointed** His eternal Son, Jesus Christ, to be the Mediator. 
* **Voluntary Role:** Christ did not have this role forced upon Him; He willingly accepted it. 
* **Endowed for the Task:** To equip Him for this office, the Father anointed Him with the Holy Spirit without measure, giving Him all power and knowledge necessary to execute His mediatorial work.

### 2. The Person of the Mediator: The Hypostatic Union (Section 2)
The Confession strongly emphasizes the **two natures** of Christ—fully God and fully man—united in one person (the Hypostatic Union).
* **Fully God:** He is the eternal Son of God, of the same substance and equal with the Father.
* **Fully Man:** In the fullness of time, He took on human nature—body and soul—with all its ordinary infirmities, yet **without sin**. He was conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin Mary.
* **The Union:** These two distinct natures (divine and human) are inseparably joined together in one person, "without conversion, composition, or confusion" (echoing the Council of Chalcedon). Because of this union, whatever Christ does in either nature is attributed to the whole person.

### 3. The Threefold Office of the Mediator (Section 1 & 3)
Christ does not mediate merely by existing; He mediates by executing three specific offices: **Prophet, Priest, and King.**
* **Prophet:** He reveals God’s will and truth to His church.
* **Priest:** He offers Himself as a sacrifice for sin, satisfies God’s justice, and makes intercession for the redeemed.
* **King:** He calls, subdues, rules, defends, and preserves His church. He also restrains and conquers all His and His church's enemies.

The Confession follows the classic Reformed order of Christ's humiliation and exaltation.
* **Humiliation:** Christ was made under the law, perfectly fulfilled it, and underwent the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross. He was buried and remained under the power of death for a time.

### 5. Active and Passive Obedience (Section 5)
This is a crucial and distinctively Reformed doctrine. The Confession teaches that Christ's mediatorial work involves two types of obedience:
* **Passive Obedience:** Christ suffered the penalty of sin (the wrath of God and death on the cross) to satisfy God's justice.
* **Active Obedience:** Christ perfectly kept the law of God throughout His life.

The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), one of the most influential documents in Reformed theology, addresses the doctrine of effectual calling in **Chapter 10**. 

"Effectual calling" refers to God's sovereign work of grace whereby He irresistibly draws His elect to salvation. It is "effectual" because it always successfully results in the conversion of the person called; it never fails.

Here is a breakdown of what the Westminster Confession teaches about effectual calling, based on its three sections:

### 1. The Agent, the Means, and the Mechanism (WCF 10.1)
The first section defines *who* does the calling, *how* He does it, and *what* happens in the human soul.

*   **The Agent:** It is solely the work of God. The Confession states that God calls those whom He has "predestinated unto life." It is not a collaborative effort where God does His part and man does his; rather, God is the primary actor.
*   **The Timing:** God calls them "in His appointed and accepted time." This highlights God's sovereignty over the exact moment of a person's conversion.
*   **The Means:** God uses the outward means of His Word (the preaching of the Gospel) and His ordinances (sacraments), but the Confession is careful to note that these outward means are completely insufficient on their own to save. 
*   **The Mechanism (The Inward Work of the Spirit):** The Holy Spirit accompanies the Word to make it effectual. The Spirit does three things:
    1.  **Enlightens the mind:** He gives spiritual understanding of the Gospel.
    2.  **Renews the will:** He changes the disposition of the heart. Because of the Fall, man's will is bound in sin and hostile to God. The Spirit removes this hostility.
    3.  **Persuades and enables:** He doesn't just show the truth; He powerfully bends the will so that the sinner is "made willing by His grace" to embrace Jesus Christ freely offered in the Gospel.

*Key Takeaway:* Effectual calling does not violate the human will; rather, it heals and renews the will so that the sinner comes to Christ willingly and joyfully, not by coercion.

### 2. The Special Case of Infants and the Incapacitated (WCF 10.2 & 10.3)
The Confession addresses two specific scenarios regarding the outward call of the Gospel:

*   **Infants and the Mentally Incapacitated:** The Confession teaches that elect infants (and those who are mentally incapable of being called by the outward ministry of the Word) are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit. The Spirit works "immediately" (directly, without the preaching of the Word as a prerequisite). The Confession does not claim *all* infants are saved, but affirms that God's grace is not bound by the ordinary means (the preaching of the Word) when a person is physically incapable of receiving them.
*   **The Unevangelized:** The Confession explicitly states that those who do not have access to the outward call of the Gospel cannot be saved, no matter how diligently they live according to the light of nature or the laws of a false religion. This upholds the Reformed doctrine of the absolute necessity of the Gospel and the Holy Spirit's work for salvation.

### 3. The Distinction Between the General Call and the Effectual Call (WCF 10.4)
The final section addresses what happens to the non-elect (those not predestined to life) when they hear the Gospel.

*   **The General Call:** The Confession acknowledges that God offers the Gospel to all who hear it outwardly. This is often called the "general" or "outward" call. God sincerely invites all who hear to repent and believe.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), completed in 1647, is the foundational doctrinal standard for Presbyterian and Reformed churches. Its teaching on justification is found primarily in **Chapter 11**, which is widely considered one of the most precise and important articulations of the Protestant doctrine of justification in church history.

Drawing heavily from the Apostle Paul (especially Romans and Galatians) and the theology of John Calvin, the WCF teaches that justification is a legal (forensic) act of God’s free grace, received by faith alone, based entirely on the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ.

Here is a breakdown of the key elements of what the Westminster Confession teaches about justification:

### 1. Justification is a Legal (Forensic) Declaration, Not an Internal Change
Section 1 makes a vital distinction between *justification* and *sanctification*. 
*   **Not Infused:** The Confession explicitly denies the Roman Catholic doctrine that God "infuses" righteousness into a person, thereby making them internally good and thus justifying them. 
*   **Pardoning and Accounting:** Instead, justification is a forensic (courtroom) act. God, as the righteous judge, does two things: He **pardons** the sinner's sins, and He **accounts** (credits) the sinner as righteous in His sight. 
*   **Not Based on Us:** This declaration is "not for anything wrought in them, or done by them." The sinner is not justified because they have become inherently good, but because their legal status before God has changed from "guilty" to "righteous."

### 2. The Ground of Justification: The Imputed Righteousness of Christ
If God does not justify us based on our own goodness, on what basis does He do it? Section 1 and 3 point entirely to Jesus Christ.
*   **Double Imputation:** The Confession teaches the classic Reformed doctrine of double imputation. The sinner's sins are imputed (credited) to Christ, who suffered the penalty for them on the cross. Conversely, Christ’s perfect obedience and righteousness are imputed (credited) to the sinner.
*   **Active and Passive Obedience:** Section 3 specifies that it is Christ’s "obedience and satisfaction" that are imputed. *Obedience* refers to His active keeping of the law throughout His life; *satisfaction* refers to His passive suffering the penalty of the law on the cross. Both are credited to the believer, meaning we are not only forgiven of our sins but are seen as having positively fulfilled the law through Christ.

### 3. The Instrument of Justification: Faith Alone
Section 2 explains *how* a sinner receives this imputed righteousness.
*   **Faith is the Instrument:** The siner is justified "by faith alone." Faith is the empty hand that receives the gift of Christ's righteousness. It is the *instrument* of justification, not the *cause* of it.
*   **Faith is Not the Righteousness:** The Confession is careful to state that faith itself is not our righteousness; rather, faith "receives and rests upon Christ and His righteousness." Even the faith to believe is a gift of God, so no one can boast.
*   **Faith is Never Alone:** While we are justified by faith *alone*, the faith that justifies is never *by itself*. True, justifying faith is "ever accompanied with all other saving graces" and "worketh by love." In other words, good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of true faith, but they play no part in earning or contributing to justification.

### 4. Justification Occurs in Time, Not Eternity
Section 4 addresses a theological debate of the 17th century regarding "eternal justification" (the idea that God justified the elect from all eternity). 
*   The Confession teaches that while God decreed the justification of the elect from eternity, and Christ purchased their justification on the cross, individuals are not actually justified until the Holy Spirit applies Christ's work to them **in time**—specifically, at the moment they believe the gospel.

### 5. Justification Under the Old Testament
Section 5 affirms the unity of the covenant of grace across redemptive history. 
*   Believers in the Old Testament were justified in the exact same way as believers in the New Testament. They looked forward by faith to the promised Messiah (through the sacrificial system), just as New Testament believers look backward to the finished work of Christ.

### 6. The Assurance of Justification
Section 5 also touches on the believer's assurance.
*   Because justification relies entirely on Christ's finished work and God's unchanging decree, believers can and should attain a sure and infallible assurance that they are justified. However, the Confession acknowledges that this assurance can fluctuate based on the believer's spiritual condition, and it may be temporarily shaken by sin or temptation, though it will ultimately be restored by the Holy Spirit.

### Summary
In short, the Westminster Confession teaches that justification is an act of God's free grace, wherein He declares a sinner to be righteous in His sight. This is not based on the sinner's own works or internal transformation, but solely on the perfect life and atoning death of Jesus Christ, whose righteousness is credited to the sinner, and which the sinner receives by faith alone.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF) provides one of the most famous and robust articulations of the doctrine of the Perseverance of the Saints in Chapter 17. This chapter balances the absolute certainty of the believer's eternal security with the serious reality of sin and backsliding, rejecting both "lose-your-salvation" theology and "carnal Christian" (antinomian) theology.

Here is a breakdown of what the WCF teaches about the perseverance of the saints:

### 1. The Certainty of Perseverance (Chapter 17, Section 1)
The Confession teaches that those whom God has genuinely called, justified, and sanctified will absolutely make it to heaven. They "can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace." 

The WCF roots this certainty not in the strength of the believer's willpower, but in the unchangeable nature of God and His salvific work. It gives four foundational reasons why true believers cannot lose their salvation:
*   **The Decree of God:** God has eternally decreed who will be saved, and His decree cannot be thwarted.
*   **The Covenant of Grace:** God has promised salvation in this covenant, and He cannot lie.
*   **Christ’s Intercession:** Jesus continually prays for His people (John 17), ensuring their faith will not fail.
*   **The Indwelling Spirit and the Seed of God:** The Holy Spirit dwells in believers, and God's "seed" (the new nature) remains in them, making apostasy impossible.

### 2. The Ground of Perseverance: God’s Power, Not Human Will (Chapter 17, Section 2)
The Confession is careful to guard against the idea that perseverance is achieved by human effort. It states that the perseverance of the saints "depends not upon their own free will, but upon the immutability of the decree of God..." 

Because salvation is rooted in the Trinity—God the Father electing, God the Son redeeming and interceding, and God the Spirit indwelling and empowering—salvation is secure. Believers persevere because God preserves them. The WCF explicitly ties this to the "covenant of grace," emphasizing that God is committed to keeping His people just as much as He calls them to keep His commandments.

### 3. The Reality of Backsliding and Temporary Falls (Chapter 17, Section 3)
Perhaps the most pastorally significant section of Chapter 17 is its "Nevertheless" clause. The WCF acknowledges that true believers *do* fall into serious sin. They can be overcome by temptations, fall into "grievous sins," and continue in them for a time. 

The Confession lists the terrible consequences of such backsliding:
*   They incur God's displeasure.
*   They grieve the Holy Spirit.
*   They are deprived of some measure of their graces and comforts.
*   They bring temporal judgments upon themselves.
*   Their hearts are hardened, and their consciances wounded.

However, even in this dark state, the WCF maintains that they will not lose their salvation. God's Fatherly displeasure is a disciplinary displeasure (like a father disciplining a child), not a condemning displeasure (like a judge condemning a criminal). Their falls are temporary and partial, not "total" or "final." God will eventually bring them to repentance and restore them.

### Key Distinctions Made by the WCF
The WCF’s doctrine of perseverance carefully navigates between two theological errors:

*   **Against Arminianism (which teaches believers can lose their salvation):** The WCF argues that salvation is secured by God's grace, not human performance. If salvation could be lost by human sin, it would mean Christ's intercession is insufficient and God's decree is changeable.
*   **Against Antinomianism / "Easy Believism" (which teaches that a person can accept Jesus and then live however they want and still go to heaven):** The WCF insists that those who fall into persistent, unrepentant sin demonstrate that they were never truly saved to begin with (1 John 2:19). True believers *will* persevere in holiness, not because they are perfect, but because the Spirit ensures they will ultimately return to the faith. 

### Summary
The Westminster Confession teaches that **true believers will certainly persevere to the end and be saved because God preserves them.** This security is based entirely on God's grace, Christ's intercession, and the Spirit's indwelling, not on human effort. However, **believers can and do fall into grievous sins**, which brings God's loving discipline and a loss of spiritual comfort, but these falls are never final. God will ultimately restore them, ensuring they never totally or finally fall away from grace.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (WCF), a foundational document of Reformed theology, outlines its doctrine of the last judgment primarily in **Chapter 33** (with supporting concepts in Chapters 8 and 32). 

The Confession’s teaching on the last judgment emphasizes the certainty of the event, the glory of Christ as Judge, the absolute justice of the verdicts, and the practical, pastoral impact this doctrine should have on believers.

Here is a breakdown of what the Westminster Confession teaches about the last judgment:

### 1. The Fact and the Judge
The Confession teaches that God has appointed a specific, future day for judgment. This will not be an ongoing process or a mere state of mind, but a definitive, historical event. 
* **Jesus Christ as Judge:** The judgment will be executed by Jesus Christ. The Father has given all judgment to the Son, and He will return in glory to judge the world. 
* **The Timing:** The exact day of this event is unknown to angels and humans, known only to God the Father. Therefore, people are to live in a state of constant watchfulness.

### 2. The Subjects of Judgment
Everyone will stand before the judgment seat of Christ. The Confession specifically mentions two groups:
* **Apostate Angels:** The fallen angels (demons) will be judged and condemned.
* **All Human Beings:** Every human being who has ever lived will appear before Christ to give an account. No one is exempt.

### 3. The Purpose of the Judgment
The primary purpose of the last judgment is not fact-finding (since God is omniscient), but the public vindication of God’s glory. The judgment will serve as the ultimate, public display of two divine attributes:
* **The Glory of God’s Mercy:** In the salvation and acquittal of the righteous, God’s immense grace and mercy will be put on display for all of creation to see.
* **The Glory of God’s Justice:** In the condemnation of the wicked and apostate angels, God’s perfect, unwavering justice and hatred of sin will be publicly vindicated.

### 4. The Outcomes of the Judgment
The Confession is unapologetically dualistic regarding the eternal outcomes—there are only two destinations, and they are everlasting.

* **The Righteous:** Those who have been justified by faith in Christ will be publicly acquitted. They will be openly acknowledged before the Father and the holy angels. They will be welcomed into eternal life and glory, entering into the fullness of joy in the presence of the Lord.
* **The Wicked:** Those who have not repented and believed will be condemned. They will be cast into eternal torment and punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His power.

### 5. The Role of "Works" in the Judgment
A crucial aspect of the WCF’s teaching is how "works" function at the judgment. The Confession maintains the classic Protestant distinction between justification by faith alone and judgment according to works:
* **The Wicked:** They will be judged "according to their works." Their sinful deeds and rejection of Christ will be the just basis for their condemnation.
* **The Righteous:** They are justified in this life solely by the imputed righteousness of Christ. However, at the last judgment, their good works will be brought forward—not as the *meritorious* cause of their salvation, but as the *evidence* and fruits of their true faith and union with Christ. 

### 6. Practical Application (The Pastoral Use of the Doctrine)
The Westminster Divines (the authors of the Confession) did not view the last judgment as mere abstract theology. Chapter 33, Section 3 explicitly states how this doctrine should be applied to the Christian life:
* **A Deterrent from Sin:** The certainty of future judgment and eternal punishment should terrify the wicked and restrain believers from falling into sin.
* **A Comfort to the Righteous:** In times of suffering, persecution, and injustice, the promise that Christ will finally right all wrongs and judge their oppressors provides profound comfort to believers.
* **A Call to Watchfulness:** Because the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, all people—especially believers—are urged to live holy, God-honoring lives, continually looking forward to the return of their Savior.

In summary, the Westminster Confession of Faith teaches that the last judgment is the grand, culminating event of history, orchestrated by Jesus Christ, designed to publicly display the glory of God's justice and mercy, resulting in the eternal, conscious blessedness of the righteous and the eternal, conscious punishment of the wicked.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession, written in 1561 by Guido de Brès, is one of the foundational doctrinal standards of Reformed Christianity. Its teaching about the "only God" is found primarily in **Article 1** (titled "There is Only One God") and is further clarified in **Article 8** (regarding the Trinity). 

Here is a breakdown of what the Belgic Confession teaches about the only God:

### 1. Strict Monotheism
The Confession begins with a clear, unequivocal declaration of monotheism: *"We all believe with the heart, and confess with the mouth, that there is one only simple and spiritual Being, which we call God."* This establishes that there is exactly one God, rejecting polytheism (many gods) and atheism (no God). 

### 2. The Nature of God: "Simple and Spiritual"
The Confession uses two very specific theological terms to describe God's nature:
*   **Spiritual:** God is immaterial. He does not have a physical body and cannot be seen with physical eyes. This echoes John 4:24 ("God is spirit").
*   **Simple:** In classical theology, "simple" does not mean God is easy to understand or unintelligent. Rather, it means God is not composed of parts. He is not made up of different ingredients (like body and soul, or different properties pasted together). His essence is entirely unified; His love *is* His justice, which *is* His holiness, which *is* His very being. 

### 3. The Attributes of God
Article 1 lists a series of attributes that describe the character and power of this one God. He is:
*   **Eternal:** He has no beginning and no end; He exists outside of time.
*   **Incomprehensible:** He cannot be fully grasped or understood by the finite human mind.
*   **Invisible:** He cannot be seen by human eyes in this life.
*   **Immutable:** He does not change; He is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
*   **Infinite:** He has no limits or boundaries.
*   **Almighty:** He possesses all power and authority.
*   **Perfectly wise, just, and good:** His moral character is absolute and flawless.

### 4. The Source of All Good
The Confession describes God as *"the overflowing fountain of all good."* This means that everything that is good, true, beautiful, and life-giving originates from God. He does not just *do* good; He *is* the very source and fountain from which all goodness flows. 

### 5. The Trinitarian Clarification (Article 8)
While Article 1 establishes that there is "one only" God, the Confession immediately follows up in Article 8 to explain *how* this one God exists: as the Trinity. It teaches that this one, simple, spiritual Being exists in three distinct Persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Confession is careful to state that these three are not three gods, but share one single, identical divine essence. 

### Summary
In short, the Belgic Confession teaches that the only God is the one, undivided, immaterial, and part-less Being who is infinite, eternal, and unchanging in His power and perfection. He is the ultimate source of all goodness, and He exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

All these things are enough to convict humans and to leave them without excuse. questions.response:
The Belgic Confession, one of the primary doctrinal standards of Reformed Christianity, addresses the means by which we know God directly in **Article 2**, titled "The Means by Which We Know God." 

The Confession teaches that God makes Himself known to humanity through **two primary means**: the universe (General Revelation) and Scripture (Special Revelation). 

Here is a detailed breakdown of what the Belgic Confession teaches about these two means:

### 1. The First Means: The "Book" of Nature (General Revelation)
The Confession teaches that the created order is the first way we know God. It uses a beautiful literary metaphor, describing the universe as an "elegant book" where all creatures, no matter how small, are like "letters" that show us who God is.

*   **What it reveals:** Through creation, preservation, and the government of the universe, we can perceive God's "invisible attributes," specifically His **eternal power** and **divinity** (godhood). 
*   **The extent of this knowledge:** The Confession states that this revelation is so clear and obvious that it leaves all human beings "without excuse." No one can claim they do not know that a powerful, divine Creator exists, because the evidence is constantly before their eyes.
*   **The limitation of this knowledge:** While nature reveals *that* God is and that He is powerful, it is insufficient to tell us *who* God is in a saving way, nor does it reveal His will for our salvation. Because of human sin and blindness, the "book of nature" cannot bring us to a saving knowledge of God.

### 2. The Second Means: The "Book" of Scripture (Special Revelation)
Because nature is insufficient for salvation, the Confession teaches that God makes Himself known "more openly" through His holy and divine Word—what we know as the Bible.

*   **What it reveals:** Scripture reveals God's will and everything that is "necessary for us to know in this life, to his glory and for our salvation." It reveals God not just as a powerful Creator, but as a loving Father, a Redeemer, and the one who saves sinners through Jesus Christ.
*   **The necessity of Scripture:** The Confession implies that without Scripture, humanity—fallen in sin—would remain in spiritual darkness regarding how to be saved and how to properly serve God.

### The Role of the Holy Spirit
While Article 2 establishes the *means* (Nature and Scripture), the Belgic Confession makes it clear in other articles (such as Article 3 on the inspiration of Scripture, and Article 5 on the authority of Scripture) that these means are only effective because of the work of the Holy Spirit. 

*   **Regarding Nature:** The Holy Spirit is the one who opens our eyes to see the glory of God in creation, preventing us from attributing the universe to chance or idols.
*   **Regarding Scripture:** The Holy Spirit is the author of the Word and the one who "testifies in our hearts" that the Scriptures are truly from God. Without the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit, the reading of Scripture alone will not produce a saving knowledge of God.

### Summary of the Relationship Between the Two Means
In the theology of the Belgic Confession, the two means of knowing God do not contradict each other; rather, they complement one another. 
*   **Nature** tells us that God exists and is infinitely powerful, leaving us without excuse for our unbelief. 
*   **Scripture** picks up where nature leaves off, telling us the character of God, our fallen condition, and the way of salvation through Jesus Christ. 

Therefore, to truly know God, we must read both "books"—the book of nature to see His majesty, and the book of Scripture to know His saving grace.

This teaching is most clearly articulated in **Article 7**, titled *"The Sufficiency of the Holy Scriptures to Be the Only Rule of Faith."* 

Along with Articles 2 through 6, Article 7 establishes the Reformed doctrine of *Sola Scriptura* (Scripture alone). Here is a breakdown of what the Belgic Confession teaches about the sufficiency of Scripture:

### 1. Scripture Contains Everything Necessary for Salvation and Worship
The Confession teaches that the Bible is entirely sufficient for its intended purpose. It states that God’s Word contains **"the whole manner of worship which God requires of us."** 
This means that believers do not need to look outside of the Bible to know how to be saved or how to live a life pleasing to God. While the Bible does not tell us everything there is to know about science, history, or mathematics, it is completely sufficient for its primary purpose: revealing everything we must believe and do to be saved.

### 2. No Additions or Subtractions are Permitted
Because Scripture is sufficient, the Confession strictly forbids adding to or taking away from God's Word. It cites Deuteronomy 4:2 and Revelation 22:18-19 to warn against altering the biblical text. Even if an apostle or an angel from heaven were to teach something contrary to Scripture, the Confession says (citing Galatians 1:8), they must be rejected. 

### 3. Human Writings are Subordinate to Scripture
Article 7 makes a crucial distinction between the Bible and all other human documents. While the Confession highly values the writings of church fathers, councils, and ancient traditions, it states:
> *"Neither may we consider any writings of men, however holy these men may have been, of equal value with those divine Scriptures, nor ought we to consider custom, or the great multitude, or antiquity, or succession of times and persons, or councils, decrees, or statutes, as of equal value with the truth of God..."*

Even the best human theological writings (including the Belgic Confession itself!) are subordinate to Scripture. They can be useful as helps, but they are not binding on the conscience in the way Scripture is.

The Confession explicitly rejects the idea that the Holy Spirit continues to give new, normative revelations that contradict or add to the Bible. How do we know the Scriptures are sufficient and true? The Confession teaches that we do not believe the Bible simply because the church tells us to. Rather, **"the Holy Spirit witnesses in our hearts that they are from God."** The sufficiency of Scripture is grasped by faith, which is worked in the believer by the internal testimony of the Spirit. questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation of all things?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that the Father, when it seemed good to him, created heaven and earth and all other creatures from nothing, by the Word- that is to say, by the Son. God has given all creatures their being, form, and appearance and their various functions for serving their Creator. Even now God also sustains and governs them all, according to his eternal providence and by his infinite power, that they may serve humanity, in order that humanity may serve God. God has also created the angels good, that they might be messengers of God and serve the elect. Some of them have fallen from the excellence in which God created them into eternal perdition; and the others have persisted and remained in their original state, by the grace of God. The devils and evil spirits are so corrupt that they are enemies of God and of everything good. They lie in wait for the church and every member of it like thieves, with all their power, to destroy and spoil everything by their deceptions. So then, by their own wickedness they are condemned to everlasting damnation, daily awaiting their torments. For that reason we detest the error of the Sadducees, who deny that there are spirits and angels, and also the error of the Manicheans, who say that the devils originated by themselves, being evil by nature, without having been corrupted.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession, written in 1561 by Guido de Brès, is one of the primary doctrinal standards of Reformed Christianity. Its teachings on the creation of all things are found specifically in **Article 12**, titled "The Creation of All Things." 

Here is a breakdown of what the Belgic Confession teaches about creation:

### 1. Creation Out of Nothing (*Creatio Ex Nihilo*)
The Confession begins by affirming that God did not form the universe out of pre-existing matter. Instead, He created all things "out of nothing" (Latin: *creatio ex nihilo*). This underscores God's absolute sovereignty and power; He didn't need any raw materials to create—He simply spoke, and it came into being.

### 2. Trinitarian Involvement
While God the Father is often spoken of as the source of creation, the Confession is explicitly Trinitarian in its view of creation. It states that the Father created all things "by his Word—that is to say, by his Son" and "in the Holy Spirit." This means creation is not the work of one Person of the Godhead, but a cooperative act of the Triune God.

### 3. The Scope of Creation: Visible and Invisible
The Confession teaches that God created "the heaven, the earth, and all creatures," making a distinction between the visible and the invisible realms. 
* **The Visible:** The physical universe, the earth, and all biological life.
* **The Invisible:** The spiritual realm, specifically the angels. 

### 4. The Creation and Nature of Angels
Article 12 spends a notable amount of time discussing angels, which was important in the 16th-century context to counter both Catholic veneration of angels and skepticism about the spiritual realm. It teaches:
* God created angels to be "ministering spirits" (servants) of God and His people.
* Angels were created good, but some fell into sin and became demons. 
* The demons are so corrupt that they are "enemies of God and of all that is good."
* Despite the existence of evil demons, God's sovereignty is not threatened; the demons are restrained by God and will ultimately face eternal condemnation.

### 5. The Original Goodness of Creation
Echoing Genesis 1, the Confession states that when God created all things, "they were all very good." It explicitly rejects the idea that physical matter is inherently evil (a common belief in ancient Gnosticism and some medieval sects). Because God created it, the physical world is fundamentally good.

### 6. The Purpose of Creation
The Confession teaches that all things were created with a specific purpose: "to serve their Creator." Creation is not an accident or an end in itself; it exists to glorify God and to function according to His divine will. 

### 7. God’s Ongoing Sustenance and Providence
A crucial aspect of the Belgic Confession's doctrine of creation is that God did not just create the world and then abandon it (Deism). It states that God "still upholds and governs [all things] by his eternal providence and infinite power." The same power that brought the universe into existence is the power that keeps it functioning moment by moment.

### 8. The Rejection of Chance or "Epicureanism"
At the end of Article 12, the Confession explicitly rejects the idea that the universe came about by chance or random collision of atoms. It mentions "Epicureans" (referring to the ancient Greek philosophy of Epicurus, which taught a materialistic, atom-based universe devoid of divine purpose). The Confession states that we must believe in God as the intentional, purposeful Creator, rejecting any notion of a self-generating universe or a Creator who is uninvolved with His creation.

### Summary
In short, the Belgic Confession teaches that the Triune God intentionally created the entire universe—both physical and spiritual—out of nothing. He created it good, for His glory, and He actively sustains and governs it, entirely rejecting the idea that the universe is the product of random chance.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of god's providence?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this good God, after creating all things, did not abandon them to chance or fortune but leads and governs them according to his holy will, in such a way that nothing happens in this world without God's orderly arrangement. Yet God is not the author of, and cannot be charged with, the sin that occurs. For God's power and goodness are so great and incomprehensible that God arranges and does his works very well and justly even when the devils and the wicked act unjustly. We do not wish to inquire with undue curiosity into what God does that surpasses human understanding and is beyond our ability to comprehend. But in all humility and reverence we adore the just judgments of God, which are hidden from us, being content to be Christ's disciples, so as to learn only what God shows us in the Word, without going beyond those limits. This doctrine gives us unspeakable comfort since it teaches us that nothing can happen to us by chance but only by the arrangement of our gracious heavenly Father, who watches over us with fatherly care, sustaining all creatures under his lordship, so that not one of the hairs on our heads (for they are all numbered) nor even a little bird can fall to the ground without the will of our Father. (Matt. 10:29-30) In this thought we rest, knowing that God holds in check the devils and all our enemies, who cannot hurt us without divine permission and will. For that reason we reject the damnable error of the Epicureans, who say that God does not get involved in anything and leaves everything to chance.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the primary doctrinal standards of Reformed Christianity, addresses the doctrine of God’s providence primarily in **Article 13** (titled "The Doctrine of God's Providence"). 

Written by Guido de Brès, this article provides a robust, comforting, and carefully nuanced definition of how God interacts with and governs His creation. Here is a breakdown of what the Belgic Confession teaches about God's providence:

### 1. The Active and Continuous Governance of God
The Confession rejects the idea of deism—that God created the world and then stepped back to let it run on its own. Instead, it teaches that God is actively and continuously involved in all things. It states that God, after creating all things, did not "forsake" them or leave them to "fortune or chance." Rather, He rules and governs them according to His holy will, so that "nothing happens in this world without his appointment." 

### 2. The Comprehensive Scope of Providence
The providence of God is not limited to "big" or "spiritual" events; it encompasses all of reality. The Confession teaches that God’s providence extends to:
*   **Human beings:** Both good and bad, believers and unbelievers.
*   **Nature:** Including animals, weather, and crops.
*   **Specific events:** Even things that appear random or trivial are under God's sovereign direction.

### 3. The Problem of Evil and the "Two Will" Distinction
One of the most difficult aspects of providence is the existence of evil and suffering. The Belgic Confession addresses this carefully to protect both God's absolute sovereignty and His perfect holiness:
*   **God is not the author of evil:** The Confession explicitly states that God is not the author of, nor can He be charged with, the sins that occur. 
*   **God permits and uses evil:** While God does not force people to sin, He allows it to happen. Furthermore, He uses even the wicked actions of humans and devils to accomplish His own righteous purposes. 
*   **The distinction of wills:** The Confession makes a crucial distinction between God's **revealed will** (what He commands, which forbids sin) and His **hidden will/decrees** (what He has ordained to happen, which includes allowing sin for a greater good). God's hands are clean, even when He uses the dirty hands of wicked humans to fulfill His plans (much like the biblical example of Joseph's brothers selling him into slavery—what they meant for evil, God meant for good).

### 4. The Reality of Secondary Causes
The Confession affirms that God's sovereign providence does not negate "secondary causes" (the natural laws and human choices through which events occur). It states that God’s providence works *through* means. For example, God provides food through the labor of farming, and healing through medicine. God is the primary cause who ordains the end, but He also ordains the means by which the end is achieved.

### 5. Human Agency and Responsibility
Because God uses secondary causes, the Confession firmly rejects the idea that God's providence turns humans into mindless robots. It explicitly states that believers are not to adopt a fatalistic attitude. It rejects the idea that God's providence makes humans into "stocks and blocks" (inanimate objects). People act freely and are morally responsible for their choices, yet those choices perfectly accomplish what God has ordained.

### 6. The Pastoral Purpose: Comfort and Trust
The ultimate goal of the doctrine of providence in the Belgic Confession is not merely philosophical, but deeply pastoral. The Confession states that this doctrine gives us "unspeakable consolation" because we know:
*   Nothing can happen to us by chance.
*   We are never separated from the love of our heavenly Father.
*   Even in suffering, persecution, or danger, God is working all things together for our salvation.

Because of this, believers are called to be **patient in adversity** and **thankful in prosperity**, trusting that God is weaving all circumstances—both good and bad—into the tapestry of His redemptive plan.

### 7. Rejection of Errors (Epicureanism)
Finally, the Confession explicitly rejects "Epicureanism"—the ancient (and modern) belief that the gods do not care about human affairs and that events are governed by random chance. It also implicitly rejects Stoic fatalism (the idea that humans are just cogs in a machine with no real agency). The Reformed view of providence stands in the middle: God is absolutely sovereign, yet intimately involved, and humans are genuinely responsible.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation and fall of humanity?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that God created human beings from the dust of the earth and made and formed them in his image and likeness- good, just, and holy; able by their will to conform in all things to the will of God. But when they were in honor they did not understand it (Ps. 49:20) and did not recognize their excellence. But they subjected themselves willingly to sin and consequently to death and the curse, lending their ear to the word of the devil. For they transgressed the commandment of life, which they had received, and by their sin they separated themselves from God, who was their true life, having corrupted their entire nature. So they made themselves guilty and subject to physical and spiritual death, having become wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all their ways. They lost all their excellent gifts which they had received from God, and retained none of them except for small traces which are enough to make them inexcusable. Moreover, all the light in us is turned to darkness, as the Scripture teaches us: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." (John 1:5) Here John calls the human race "darkness." Therefore we reject everything taught to the contrary concerning human free will, since humans are nothing but the slaves of sin and cannot do a thing unless it is given them from heaven. (John 3:27) For who can boast of being able to do anything good by oneself, since Christ says, "No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me"? (John 6:44) Who can glory in their own will when they understand that "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"? (Rom. 8:7) Who can speak of their own knowledge in view of the fact that "those who are unspiritual do not receive the gifts of God's Spirit"? (1 Cor. 2:14) In short, who can produce a single thought, knowing that we are not able to think a thing about ourselves, by ourselves, but that "our competence is from God"? (2 Cor. 3:5) And therefore, what the apostle says ought rightly to stand fixed and firm: God works within us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure. (Phil. 2:13) For there is no understanding nor will conforming to God's understanding and will apart from Christ's involvement, as he teaches us when he says, "Apart from me you can do nothing." (John 15:5)
